Melodic Analysis: Practice for Chapter 11

Exercises for Chapter 11 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom: motives and the book’s seven melodic alterations (inversion, intervallic change, augmentation, diminution, rhythmic change, ornamentation, extension, retrograde), fragments, phrases and subphrases, with themes from the site’s Classical Themes collection and the book’s listening examples.

This page goes with Chapter 11, Melodic Analysis of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first. The book is the reference for the terms used here. It builds on Chapter 10, Non-Chord Tones, which you need for ornamentation.

The book takes a melody apart at four sizes, smallest first: the motive, which can be split into fragments; and the phrase, which can be split into subphrases. The drills here are about motives and how they change. Phrases and subphrases are practised by listening, with the book’s clips, and by looking at themes in the site’s Classical Themes collection.

For writing your own motives and developing them, see the lesson Composing 2: Developing a Motif.

11.1 Motive

A motive (or motif) is the smallest melodic idea you can recognize as itself. It is usually two to seven notes, and it is recognized by its rhythm and shape more than by its exact pitches. A composer develops a motive: repeats it, moves it to other notes, changes it.

The book’s example is the first theme of Beethoven’s Symphony No. 1, where it finds four motives in four bars. Here is the theme with the book’s labels (the book’s Figure 11.1.1, engraved for this page; the Classical Themes collection has the same theme from its first downbeat, without the opening run):

  • Motive 1: a quick run down four steps to a long C.
  • Motive 2: a dotted pickup, G up to B, into C. It comes twice.
  • Motive 3: four short notes, C C G B, also twice.
  • Motive 4: a scale of quarter notes rising through the C major chord and up to C.

Later in the movement Beethoven takes each motive out of the theme and builds whole passages from it, usually as a sequence: the same motive repeated higher or lower. The book’s clips follow each one:

NoteListen: the theme, and what Beethoven does with each motive

Try it: the opening of Beethoven’s Fifth (Classical Themes, two themes) is one of the most famous motives there is. How many notes is it? Where does it come back, and what changes when it does?

TipOne answer

Four notes: three short repeated notes and a long note a 3rd below. It comes straight back a step lower, as a sequence. In the next three bars only the three short notes are kept, each time after a rest, and they climb: G, then A♭, then up to E♭. Then the line falls to a long C. That keeps a fragment of the motive (11.3). This analysis is the site’s, not the book’s.

11.2 Melodic alteration

The book names seven ways to change a motive. Move it to other notes and keep its shape, and it is a sequence. The book does not count that as an alteration, because it is so common. So the drill offers Sequence as an answer too, and you have to tell it apart from the real changes.

Alteration What changes What stays
Inversion every interval turned upside down (up becomes down) the rhythm
Intervallic change some intervals (not all), so the shape changes a little the rhythm
Augmentation every note twice as long the intervals
Diminution every note half as long the intervals
Rhythmic change some of the note lengths the notes
Ornamentation notes added between the motive’s notes (passing tones, neighbor tones) the motive’s notes, the length
Extension notes added at the end the whole motive, at the start
Retrograde the order: the notes from last to first the notes

The book’s inversions in tonal music are tonal: mirrored by steps of the scale, so a major 3rd may become a minor 3rd. The drill’s inversions are tonal too. Read 11.2

In the drill: bar 1 is the motive, bar 2 the changed copy. Press ▶ Hear it to hear both. Start with the changes you can see at a glance:

Changes of rhythm:

Changes that add or alter notes:

The book’s own example of rhythmic change is the Pathétique Sonata. In the slow introduction, motive 1 is a dotted figure. It is heard here as the top line, as in the Classical Themes collection. The book marks motive 1 from the second note of each bar:

In the development section the motive comes back with its rhythm changed. In the next bar it is shortened and moved up a step.

11.3 Fragment

Some motives are compound: long enough to break into smaller pieces, called fragments (some writers say “germs”). Each fragment can then be developed on its own. The book’s example is the seven-note motive that opens Bach’s Invention No. 1. It splits into two four-note fragments that overlap (they share the middle note). Bach later augments the first and inverts the second. Read 11.3

Listen back to the Beethoven Fifth example above: after the first two statements, only the three repeated notes are kept. That is a fragment of the motive.

NoteListen: Bach, Invention No. 1, the two fragments developed

11.4 Phrase

A phrase is the smallest section that sounds complete. In classical music a phrase ends with a cadence (Chapter 7). In popular music a phrase may end without one: the melody reaches four bars, or a line of the lyric ends. Most phrases are four bars long, some eight. Five, six and seven bars also happen, and three is rare. Read 11.4

Listen and count: play each clip and count the bars until the music sounds finished. The book’s answers are in the captions, under Answer.

11.5 Subphrase

A subphrase is bigger than a motive and smaller than a phrase. It is usually two bars, half of a four-bar phrase. Other books call it a phrase segment or phrase member. The book labels subphrases with letters. A repeat with small changes gets a prime: a′ (“a prime”), then a″. A subphrase that is only transposed keeps its letter (a, not a′). Read 11.5

Try it: label the subphrases of this Schubert theme (Classical Themes; two bars each):

TipOne answer

a (bars 1–2). a′ (bars 3–4): the same rhythm, but it starts on A, a step lower, and the leap up to F is bigger (a 4th instead of a 3rd). a″ (bars 5–6): bar 5 is bar 1 moved up a 4th, but the held note at the end is replaced by running eighth notes down from A. You could also argue that bars 5–6 are new (b) because of the eighth notes. This analysis is the site’s, not the book’s.

NoteListen: the book’s subphrase examples

NoteFor teachers
  • Links with your settings: open a drill’s Settings, then Copy a link with these settings. Add &lock=1 for a test, &count=20 for a score.
  • The drill: a motive of two to six notes filling half a bar of 4/4, in a major or minor key (natural minor), then one change of it. The answers are the book’s seven alterations, with augmentation and diminution counted separately, plus Sequence. Inversion, augmentation and diminution may also be transposed. The other changes start on the motive’s own first note (retrograde on its last), so only the change itself differs. A question is asked only when exactly one answer fits, which the drill checks before asking. Ornamentation adds one passing tone or neighbor tone and keeps the motive’s length. Retrograde reverses the pitches and the rhythm.
  • Checked: node tests/lessons/motive-drill.test.js reads thousands of questions back from their notation and classifies each change with its own code. Exactly one alteration must fit, and it must be the answer. It also checks the bar lengths and that the notes played are the notes drawn.
  • Not drilled: fragments, phrases and subphrases. Recognizing them needs real melodies, and the analysis is often open to argument (the book says so for subphrases). They are taught with the book’s clips and short examples from the Classical Themes collection.
  • Analyses: the Beethoven Symphony No. 1 motives and the Pathétique motive are the book’s (Figures 11.1.1 and 11.2.8). The answers for the Beethoven Fifth and Schubert examples are the site’s own. The themes come from the Musical Theme Dataset (Barlow and Morgenstern’s themes, newly engraved; CC BY 4.0), as credited on the Classical Themes page.
  • Videos: the clips use the book’s YouTube links and start and end times. Each title was checked against YouTube.
